chunks: "It depends what I need: resolution, whether it has to know where it is at power-up, and what it costs. I think of it as three families. First, direct angle sensors.
A potentiometer on the shaft is the cheap one: read the wiper with an ADC and you get absolute angle over maybe 270 degrees.
A magnetic angle sensor, a Hall array under a magnet on the shaft, gives 12 bits or more, absolute, contactless, and can go all the way round 360.
An optical or magnetic absolute encoder does the same with higher resolution. Resolvers are the rugged option in harsh environments. Second, incremental encoders.
An optical quadrature encoder counts steps from where it started, so I need a homing routine or an index pulse.
Resolution is great and it's cheap, but it forgets position at power-off. Third, sensorless or implicit. A stepper counts steps and, as long as it doesn't skip, that's position.
Brushless motors have Hall sensors that give about 60 electrical degrees of position, which is enough for commutation but not for precision.
And with brushed motors I can integrate speed or count commutator ripple.
Then there's a gear ratio: put the sensor on the motor shaft and the resolution at the output is multiplied by the gear ratio, but backlash means I don't know the true output position."
